title: Disasters That Changed the World · Episode 1
chapters: Pompeii and Herculaneum: towns frozen in time

units.t: Disasters That Changed the World. Episode one.
In this episode: The Bronze Age collapse, Pompeii and Herculaneum: towns frozen in time and The Great Fire of London.
Part one. The Bronze Age collapse.
Around 1200 BC, a connected world of kingdoms around the eastern Mediterranean fell apart within a few generations.
Palaces burned, writing vanished in places, and historians still debate why.
A connected ancient world.
In the 1300s BC, the eastern Mediterranean was surprisingly connected.
Egypt, the Hittites in Anatolia, Babylon, Assyria, the Mycenaean Greeks and trading cities such as Ugarit on the Syrian coast exchanged goods, gifts and letters.
Diplomatic letters found at Amarna in Egypt, mostly in Akkadian cuneiform, show kings calling one another 'brother' and haggling over gold, horses and royal marriages.
Palaces at the centre of these kingdoms ran complex economies, recording grain, livestock and workers on clay tablets.
Like modern globalised systems, this one depended on many parts working together at once.
Bronze needed the world.
Bronze is copper mixed with a little tin, roughly one part tin to nine parts copper.
Copper was fairly available, with Cyprus a major source.
Tin was much rarer and often had to travel huge distances, possibly from Central Asia among other sources.
The whole Bronze Age economy therefore depended on long trade routes.
A shipwreck found off Uluburun in southern Turkey, from the late 1300s BC, shows how rich that trade was.
It carried about ten tonnes of copper ingots and about a tonne of tin, along with glass, ivory, ebony, gold jewellery and goods from at least half a dozen cultures.
Bronze, and power, rested on fragile networks.
Palaces fall, raiders arrive.
In the decades around 1200 BC, things began to break.
Mycenaean palaces such as Pylos burned.
The Hittite capital Hattusa was abandoned and burned, and the Hittite kingdom disappeared.
Ugarit was destroyed and never rebuilt.
Not everywhere fell at once, but by about 1150 BC the old system had collapsed.
Egypt survived, shrunken, and Assyria and Babylon endured in reduced form.
In Greece, Linear B writing stopped and literacy was lost for centuries.
Ramesses III's temple at Medinet Habu records a victory over invaders from the sea, around 1177 BC.
Carvings show warriors and families in ox carts, suggesting migration.
Historians call them the Sea Peoples, and many now see them as a symptom as much as a cause.
A perfect storm.
Pollen, lake sediments and cave formations point to drier conditions in the eastern Mediterranean at this time.
Texts mention grain shortages: the Hittites asked Egypt for grain, and one letter urgently asks Ugarit for ships to carry food.
Some researchers also argue that earthquakes struck over several decades.
Any one pressure might have been survivable.
Together they strained palace economies that relied on food surplus.
Historians such as Eric Cline, in his book '1177 BC', describe a 'perfect storm'.
In a tightly connected system, a shock in one place spreads.
If tin stopped arriving, bronze tools could not be made.
If grain failed, cities went hungry.
If palaces fell, the scribes, craftsmen and traders who depended on them scattered.
This is called systems collapse.
What came after.
The centuries that followed are sometimes called a dark age, partly because written records become scarce.
Population fell and many settlements shrank.
Yet the collapse also cleared space for new things.
Iron, made from widely available ore rather than imported tin, gradually came into wide use, giving the Iron Age its name.
Smaller states emerged, including the Phoenician cities, the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, and new Aramaean states.
Phoenician traders spread a simple alphabet of about two dozen letters, much easier to learn than cuneiform or hieroglyphs.
The Greeks later adapted it, and the Latin letters you are reading now descend from it.
Connected systems bring wealth, but they can also fall together.
The key idea: Around 1300 BC the eastern Mediterranean kingdoms formed an early globalised system of trade and diplomacy.
Part two. Pompeii and Herculaneum: towns frozen in time.
In AD 79 a volcano buried two Roman towns in a matter of hours.
What it destroyed, it also preserved: bread in the oven, graffiti on the walls and the last moments of the people who lived there.
A mountain nobody feared.
Picture a busy market town on the Bay of Naples, vineyards climbing the slopes of a green mountain behind it.
To the Romans, Vesuvius was good farming land.
It had not erupted in living memory.
Pompeii had perhaps 10,000 to 12,000 residents, while nearby Herculaneum was a smaller, wealthier seaside town.
In AD 62 a strong earthquake shook the region, and some buildings were still being repaired when Vesuvius erupted.
Nobody connected the tremors with what was coming.
The traditional date is 24 August, but clues such as autumn fruit and a charcoal inscription suggest it may have been October.
That ignorance is why the eruption was so deadly, and why so much was left exactly where it stood.
The day the sky fell.
Around midday, Vesuvius blasted a column of ash and pumice skyward.
Pliny the Younger, about 17 and watching from Misenum across the bay, compared its shape to an umbrella pine.
For hours pumice rained on Pompeii, collapsing many roofs.
Overnight and into the next morning, the column collapsed and sent pyroclastic surges down the mountain: avalanches of superheated gas and ash faster than anyone could run.
Herculaneum, closer to the volcano but upwind of the pumice, was hit by these surges and buried under metres of material that hardened into rock.
Pliny's two letters to the historian Tacitus are our only surviving eyewitness record.
They describe darkness 'like a sealed room'.
His uncle, Pliny the Elder, commander of the Roman fleet, died at Stabiae.
Bodies in the ash.
As the ash around Pompeii's victims hardened, their bodies decayed, leaving hollow spaces shaped exactly like the people who had been there.
In 1863, the archaeologist Giuseppe Fiorelli had the idea of pouring liquid plaster into these cavities.
When the plaster set and the ash was chipped away, the casts showed people curled up, shielding their faces, or holding one another.
Even a dog straining at its chain was preserved.
Herculaneum told a different story.
For centuries experts assumed most people had escaped, until hundreds of skeletons were found in the 1980s, crowded into boathouses by the old shoreline, apparently waiting for rescue by sea.
Their bones now reveal Roman health, diet and injuries.
Graffiti and takeaway.
Walk down a Pompeii street today and you pass stepping stones for crossing roads, ruts worn by cart wheels and dozens of street-food counters called thermopolia, with big jars set into stone benches.
Many Romans lived in small apartments and did not cook at home, so a hot meal on the street was normal.
The walls carry painted election notices urging votes for local candidates, and thousands of scratched graffiti: jokes, insults, love notes, boasts and records of debts.
Bakeries hold millstones, ovens and carbonised loaves.
Grand homes like the House of the Vettii have colourful frescoes, and one doorway mosaic shows a fierce dog with the words 'Cave canem', meaning 'beware of the dog'.
Reading the unreadable.
After the eruption the towns were forgotten, buried under new soil and later villages.
Formal excavations began at Herculaneum in 1738 and at Pompeii in 1748.
Early digging was more treasure hunt than science, but methods improved.
A luxurious villa at Herculaneum held a library of papyrus scrolls, turned into fragile black lumps by the heat, and attempts to unroll them destroyed many.
Recently, researchers have scanned scrolls with powerful X-rays and used machine learning to spot faint traces of ink.
In 2023 and 2024, teams revealed passages of Greek philosophy unread for nearly 2,000 years.
Excavation continues, and tourism and weather threaten the ruins.
Vesuvius remains active, with hundreds of thousands living nearby, so Italy monitors it and maintains evacuation plans.
The key idea: The people of Pompeii did not recognise Vesuvius as a volcano, so the AD 79 eruption caught them unprepared.
Part three. The Great Fire of London.
In September 1666 a small fire in a bakery grew into a firestorm that swallowed a medieval city.
What rose from the ashes still shapes London today.
A city built to burn.
Sometime after midnight on Sunday 2 September 1666, a fire started in Thomas Farriner's bakery on Pudding Lane, near London Bridge.
Farriner insisted he had put out his oven, but the house was soon ablaze.
The Lord Mayor, Sir Thomas Bludworth, reportedly decided the blaze was not worth demolishing neighbouring houses for.
It was a costly misjudgement.
London was still largely medieval.
Houses were timber and plaster, with overhanging upper storeys that almost touched across narrow streets.
Rubbish, hay and firewood lay everywhere.
Firefighting meant leather buckets, axes, hand pumps and hooks for pulling buildings down, with no organised brigade.
The summer had been dry and a strong east wind was blowing.
When the fire reached warehouses on the Thames full of oil, tallow, coal and brandy, it grew too hot to approach.
Four days, two diarists.
For about four days the fire swept west and north.
People fled with what they could carry, piling belongings into carts and boats.
St Paul's Cathedral, covered in wooden scaffolding for repairs, caught fire, and its lead roof reportedly ran down the streets.
King Charles II and his brother James, Duke of York, helped create firebreaks by pulling down or blowing up houses.
When the wind eased on Tuesday night, the firebreaks held, and the fire was under control by Wednesday and Thursday.
We know much of this from Samuel Pepys and John Evelyn.
Pepys watched from a boat, noting pigeons that hovered around their homes until their wings caught fire.
He also buried his wine and parmesan cheese in his garden.
Evelyn described the ground so hot it was hard to walk on.
Counting the cost.
About 13,000 houses were destroyed, along with 87 parish churches, St Paul's Cathedral, the Guildhall and many other public buildings.
Tens of thousands of people were homeless, camping in the fields north of the city.
Only a handful of deaths were officially recorded, but historians think the true number was higher, since the poor, or anyone consumed by intense heat, may never have been counted.
People wanted someone to blame.
Foreigners and Catholics were attacked in the streets.
A French watchmaker named Robert Hubert confessed to starting the fire and was hanged, even though evidence later suggested he had not been in London when it began.
Fear ran high: London had lost perhaps a fifth of its people to the Great Plague of 1665.
An inquiry eventually concluded the fire was an accident.
Rebuilding London.
Within days, Christopher Wren and John Evelyn presented plans for a new London with wide boulevards and open piazzas.
None was adopted.
Property owners wanted their land back quickly, and sorting out who owned what was hard enough already.
The city was rebuilt largely along its old street pattern, with important changes.
New laws required buildings of brick or stone, set limits on heights and widened some streets.
Wren designed the new St Paul's Cathedral with its famous dome, which took decades to complete, and dozens of new city churches.
A special Fire Court settled disputes between landlords and tenants so rebuilding could get moving.
The long shadow.
Near Pudding Lane stands the Monument, a stone column designed by Wren and Robert Hooke.
It is 202 feet, roughly 61 metres, high, and stands about 202 feet from where the bakery was.
The fire also helped launch modern property insurance: in the following years businesses began offering cover against fire, and some ran their own teams of firefighters to protect insured buildings.
A popular story says the fire ended the plague by burning the rats, but historians doubt it.
The plague was already declining and also faded in areas the fire never touched.
What is certain is that the disaster changed how cities thought about fire safety, building materials and planning, lessons that later shaped building codes around the world, including in Australia.
The key idea: A small bakery fire in 1666 spread because London's timber houses, narrow lanes and warehouses were perfect fuel.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What did the diplomatic letters found at Amarna reveal about the Late Bronze Age?
Answer. Kings wrote to one another and swapped gifts in a connected world.
Question two. Why was Pompeii so unprepared for the eruption?
Answer. They did not see Vesuvius as a volcano or link the tremors.
Question three. Why did flames spread so easily between London's houses?
Answer. Timber houses packed along narrow lanes.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
